summary: A note from UCSB describing two commands, Login and Logout, for its Simple Minded File System, which let a user identify themselves and name an account for billing. It restates and completes RFC 399, adding a description of the responses these commands produce. It is a local service description, not a general standard.

eli5.summary: A school computer asked visitors to sign in with their name before using its filing cabinet, and to sign out when done. This note explains how.

subtitle: Two commands that let a user identify themselves and an account to UCSB's Simple Minded File System.

tldr.problem: UCSB's Simple Minded File System (SMFS) had no way to record who was using it or which account to bill, and the earlier description in RFC 399 was incomplete.
tldr.mechanism: A Login command (LGI, op code 13) gives a user name and account number, and a Logout command (LGO, op code 14) ends that association. Each gets an eight-bit completion code in reply.
tldr.outcome: This RFC restates RFC 399, adds the response codes, and obsoletes RFC 399. It is a local service description rather than a general standard.

today: RFC 431 obsoletes RFC 399 and updates RFC 122. It describes a local 1972 service at UCSB, and the unit metadata lists its status as Unknown.

sections.title: What This Note Replaces
sections.content: This document replaces RFC 399, which introduced the Login and Logout commands for UCSB's SMFS but was incomplete. RFC 399 is restated, followed by a description of the responses the commands produce. It also updates RFC 122.
sections.eli5: This is a fuller version of an earlier note that left out what the computer says back.

sections.title: Login (LGI)
sections.content:
Login is how the user identifies themselves and names the account number to be billed. It should be issued right after the ICP and before any command referencing a file. The name and account stay in effect until another LGI, an LGO, or the connection closing.

At present SMFS use is not billed, so the command is optional, the user name can be any name that identifies the user, and the account number is arbitrary. Users are asked to start using it so statistics can be collected first.

The command is an 8-bit op code (decimal 13) followed by a user name and an account number. Each is an 8-bit length followed by characters. The user name is at most eight characters, the account number at most four, both from the same character set as filenames.
sections.eli5: You say your name and a short number when you arrive. Right now the number can be anything, because nobody is being charged yet.

sections.title: Logout (LGO) and Responses
sections.content:
Logout ends the association between the user and the accounting information from the last LGI. It does not close the connection. It is not necessary before another LGI or before closing. It is currently optional and does not affect file access. Its format is just the op code, decimal 14.

Each command gets as its only response an eight-bit completion code, equal to the command's op code on success. Error codes in decimal are: 47 user name length zero, 48 user name too long, 49 user name has invalid characters, 50 account number length zero, 51 account number too long, 52 account number has invalid characters, 53 invalid user, 54 invalid account.
sections.eli5: Signing out just ends your name tag. The computer answers each command with a number: the command's own number means it worked, and other numbers say what went wrong.

items.label: Error
items.desc: User name specifies an invalid user.

items.label: Error
items.desc: Account number specifies an invalid account.
